_comment: The revise blocks: what each note section says, in the form a student can read
the night before. One block per section, keyed by its heading text as a slug.
Keys were the section's number until the sub-numbers came off the headings
("2.1.1 How RPC works in ten steps" is now "How RPC works in ten steps"), so
every key is a slug of the heading, in the same shape `reviseKey` in engine.js
derives from the page. A number as a key would silently stop matching.
The Simulation site at the repository root is the model: a heading, the answer in
a sentence, then the terms and numbers as bullets - about 60 words for a section
that here runs to 250. The prose below the block stays exactly as it is, so the
block is a second way into the same section rather than a replacement for it, and
`tools/revise_blocks.py` refuses to write a block whose bolded terms do not appear
in that section's own text. Nothing here is allowed to say something the notes do
Every edit is reviewed, not derived. Deriving these from the notes was measured
and rejected once already (see tools/dcc_slide_notes.json): a machine summary of
this material is the section heading glued to its first sentence.

ch2.js.2.0:
Distributed objects are objects in different address spaces that share data and invoke each other's methods.

  • The objects are the communicating entities, not raw bytes.
  • Location transparency is what the abstraction buys, and why distributed objects communicate by RMI.
  • A local object and a distributed object are not equivalent.
ch2.js.where-a-local-object-and-a-distributed-o:
Six areas separate a local object from a distributed one:

  • Reference — one machine word locally; it must be meaningful in another address space remotely.
  • Request latency — every call crosses a network, and it is variable.
  • Object activation — the object may not be instantiated yet.
  • Parallelism — calls can arrive from several clients at once.
  • Failure — partial failure, which produces the whole of call semantics.
  • Security — the operating system no longer enforces it; the middleware does.
ch2.js.2.1:
RPC: the client invokes a procedure that resides remotely, the server executes it and returns the result, and the caller is blocked until the reply arrives.

  • Built on the single-process procedure-call model, so it is a high-level interface.
  • The server exposes a service interface and works under a request–reply protocol: the request names a procedure, not an object.
  • Simple RPC does not keep access transparency; the stub layer fixes that.
ch2.js.2.2:
RMI: method invocation between objects in different processes. Objects that receive remote invocations are remote objects.

  • Where RPC invokes a procedure by name and drops the object reference, RMI keeps the object.
  • The caller holds a reference to an object in another process and calls a method on it.
  • That difference is what forces the proxy, the skeleton and the remote reference module.
ch2.js.2.3: RPC and RMI hide the message. Two mechanisms sit underneath them: the message-passing model, where the programmer writes the sends and receives, and serialization, which lets a structured value go into a message at all.
ch2.js.how-rpc-works-in-ten-steps:
Ten steps: 1–3 client, 4–7 server, 8–10 reply. The client procedure is blocked from step 1 until the reply arrives.

  • Marshalling — step 2: the client stub packs the parameters and the procedure name into a message.
  • Unmarshalling — step 5: the server stub unpacks them and calls the server.
  • Neither procedure knows it crossed a network.
ch2.js.advantages-and-disadvantages:
Four benefits and three costs, and each benefit is bought with its matching cost.

  • Benefits: the procedure runs in another process or on another machine; process and thread models; access transparency with a complete stub layer; code reusability.
  • Costs: call-by-value and call-by-reference only; overheads of marshalling, the round trip and kernel calls; both ends must agree the representation.
ch2.js.rpc-issues-the-five-things-that-go-wrong:
Five RPC faults, each with the mechanism that answers it:

  • The server cannot be located → a naming or binder service.
  • Lost request → retransmit after a timeout.
  • Lost reply → retransmit, or keep a history of results.
  • Server crash → duplicate filtering and idempotent operation design.
  • Client crash → the orphan call is detected and discarded.

Under these faults, call semantics decide when and how often a procedure is executed.
ch2.js.call-semantics:
Five semantics, from the ideal to the cheapest; the repair for repeats is an idempotent operation.

  • Exactly once — the ideal: time-outs, retransmission, one call identifier, a cache at the callee.
  • At most once, also called maybe — once or not at all, and the client cannot tell which.
  • At least once — one or more times; safe only when repeating is harmless.
  • Last once — the most recent call's result counts.
  • Last-of-many — accepted only if the identifier matches the newest call; orphans neglected.
ch2.js.providing-a-reliable-request-reply-proto:
Three fault-tolerant measures, each a decision with a cost:

  • Retry request message — costs the at-least-once hazard.
  • Duplicate filtering — costs state and time at the server.
  • Retransmission of results — costs stored results.

The third is the fix for a lost reply: the work was already done, so re-executing is exactly wrong.
ch2.js.what-a-remote-invocation-requires:
Three requirements, in the order a remote invocation meets them:

  • A remote object reference for the object.
  • A remote interface — only its methods can be invoked from outside; everything else is private to the process.
  • A remote object: the class implements it, with the implementation separated from what is exposed.
ch2.js.the-rmi-software:
Five roles to name when explaining RMI's architecture:

  • Proxy — marshals arguments, forwards, receives, unmarshals; from the client's side it is the object.
  • Dispatcher — receives requests and selects the correct method.
  • Skeleton — unmarshals, invokes the method, marshals the result.
  • Remote reference module — translates local to remote references and keeps the remote object table.
  • Binder — maps textual names to remote object references; servers register, clients look up.
ch2.js.the-remote-interface:
The remote interface is the boundary of what can be invoked from outside. The contrast is what each one buys:

  • CORBA — an IDL, language-neutral, so implementations may be C++ or Java. At-most-once semantics, and maybe for methods with no result.
  • Java RMI — the interface extends Remote; convenient, but both ends must be Java. At-most-once semantics.
ch2.js.design-issues-in-rmi:
RMI shares RPC's issues in three respects — interfaces, call semantics, transparency — and adds two: the invocation semantics, and how much remoteness to hide.

  • Exactly once — the ideal.
  • Maybe — the invoker cannot tell whether it ran.
  • At-least-once — a result or an exception; the hazard is arbitrary failure, repaired by idempotent operations.
  • At-most-once — a result or an exception, with nothing executed twice.

Java RMI and CORBA: at-most-once. CORBA also: maybe. SUNRPC: at-least-once.
ch2.js.location-transparency:
Full location transparency causes failure and latency, because a remote invocation differs from a local one.

  • Access transparency — the same operation is used on a remote object as on a local one. RPC delivers this.
  • Location transparency — the caller does not know where the object is. This is the claim that fails in practice.
  • Two repairs: carry the difference into the language as exceptions, or choose a weaker invocation semantics deliberately.
ch2.js.java-rmi-case-study:
Java RMI extends the Java object model to distributed objects: remote methods are called with local syntax and type checking applies equally. Its costs: single-language, and the object's behaviour under concurrency must be considered.

  • HelloInterface.java — the remote interface, extends Remote.
  • Hello.java — the remote object, extends UnicastRemoteObject implements HelloInterface.
  • HelloClient.java — Naming.lookup, then say called like a local object.
  • HelloServer.java — installs the security manager and rebinds with the rmiregistry.
ch2.js.shared-memory-versus-distributed-memory:
Two memory models, each with one advantage and one limit:

  • Shared memory — all processing elements see one data area. Easy to parallelise; practical only up to a certain system size.
  • Distributed memory — each element has its own memory and they meet only on a network. Locality is explicit and it is cheap to build; data moves only when a message says so.
ch2.js.the-message-passing-model:
The model: the work unit is the process, data units are decomposed with no shared data, and coordination is by send and recv. The analogy is mail.

  • Two details of the signature: recv may report the number of bytes received, and tag and proc may be wildcarded.
  • A specific send paired with a wildcarded receive is the request–reply interaction of 2.1.
ch2.js.collective-calls-and-spmd:
SPMD — Single Program, Multiple Data: all processors run the same program, but not in lockstep.

  • It is one program, not one per processor: each copy behaves differently from its own identity, passed in as an argument.
  • Collective calls add global reductions such as max and sum, and broadcast.
  • A collective call is also a synchronisation, so the slowest participant sets the pace.
ch2.js.mpi-the-real-message-passing-system:
MPI is the real message-passing system. Every program is bracketed by MPI_Init and MPI_Finalize, and all calls lie between them.

  • MPI_Comm_size — the number of processes.
  • MPI_Comm_rank — which part of the work this process owns.
  • MPI_Send and MPI_Recv — buffer, count, datatype, destination or source, tag, communicator.
ch2.js.what-implementing-message-passing-actual:
A send and a receive copy data from the user's space on one processor to the user's space on another, with the MPI library in between to packetize it. The known costs:

  • Data copying — paid twice, into buffers at both ends.
  • Buffer availability — a send may block if no buffer is free at the receiver.
  • Packetization, tag matching, and a progress engine.
  • Transfer needs synchronisation: the receiver may have to answer “may I send?” before the data moves.
ch2.js.messaging-protocols-short-eager-and-rend:
A message is an envelope — tag, communicator, length, source — plus data. Three protocols, trading buffer memory against waiting:

  • Short — the whole message fits in an internal buffer; lowest overhead.
  • Eager — sent as soon as it is available, whether or not the receiver is ready; best latency, at the cost of buffering.
  • Rendezvous — the header goes first and the data follows only after an ok-to-send reply; no large buffer, at the cost of a round trip.

One implementation uses all three, choosing per message.
ch2.js.persistence-and-synchronicity:
Persistence and synchronicity decide how a message is handled. Both assume applications run on hosts, one connection each to a communication server, with buffers on the hosts or in the servers.

  • Transient — discarded if it cannot be delivered now; persistent — stored until the receiver can take it.
  • Asynchronous — the sender continues immediately; synchronous — it blocks until the message is buffered or delivered.
  • Client/server computing is synchronous: the client cannot work while it waits. Queued messages are the answer.
ch2.js.serialization:
Every mechanism here has to put a structured value into a byte stream and rebuild it at the other end.

  • Marshalling — packaging arguments or a result into a message: step 2 on the client, step 7 on the server.
  • Unmarshalling — unpacking it: step 5, step 10.
  • Serialization — the general problem; marshalling is serialization for a call.
  • Representation mismatch — byte order, integer width and float format must be agreed, which is why an IDL matters.
  • A value can be copied; a pointer cannot — RPC's call-by-reference disadvantage.
ch2.js.sockets:
Sockets are the primitive under everything above: channels made across a network with the operating system's help, each thread creating an endpoint at its end.

  • The client's socket names a local I/O port, the destination machine, and the port bound to the server.
  • The server's socket names a local port; the client requests a connection, the server accepts it.
  • Java: Socket and ServerSocket, with streams so reading and writing look like file I/O.
  • A read normally blocks; setSoTimeout gives a timeout, after which the socket stays valid.
ch2.js.why-web-services-exist:
The problem: the clients, the database and the servers sit behind firewalls, so a direct connection over the Internet is normally not possible. A web service is the standard way to get data over standard web protocols, chiefly HTTP.

  • It is not that HTTP is the best transport; it is what a firewall will let through.
  • Properties: it is an API, cross-platform, implementable in most languages, and built on standard web technology.
  • The standards are defined by the W3C.
ch2.js.the-two-generations-and-their-stacks:
Web Services 1.0 uses SOAP; Web Services 2.0 uses REST. Both stacks sit on HTTP, and only the top three layers change:

  • SOAP: WSDL describes the API in machine-readable form, SOAP wraps each message in an XML envelope, the payload is XML.
  • REST: the payload is usually JSON, the meta-information rides in the HTTP headers, and WADL is completely optional and rarely used.

Fewer layers to parse and no contract to read make REST lightweight; the missing contract is what it gives up.
ch2.js.soap-versus-rest:
SOAP envelopes its own message inside the HTTP message; REST uses the standard HTTP methods — GET, PUT, POST, DELETE — as the operations, with meta-information in the headers.

  • Data: SOAP is XML-based; REST is used with XML, JSON or whatever is necessary, usually JSON.
  • Description: WSDL is required; WADL is optional and rarely used.
  • Speed: REST is faster. Maturity: SOAP carries more functionality, but is not suitable for browser-based clients.
ch2.js.a-3-tier-architecture-with-a-web-service:
The worked example: web server → web services → business logic → data source, in a presentation, a logic and a foundations layer, installed on one or more servers in your LAN or in the cloud.

  • The application tier is exposed to the world as an API.
  • Because the tier is reached over ordinary HTTP, where that tier runs stops mattering.

ch1.js.1.1:
A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing elements that appears to its users as a single coherent system.

  • Autonomous: each node keeps its own clock, decides for itself, and can fail on its own, so nothing is in charge of the whole.
  • Single coherent system: the user need not know which machine holds a file, how many machines are involved, or that any of them are remote.
  • Components communicate and coordinate their actions only by passing messages.
ch1.js.1.2:
Four goals: resource sharing, openness, transparency and scalability.

  • Resource sharing: remote data, files, printers, processors and storage used efficiently.
  • Openness: services specified through standard rules and an interface written in an IDL, which is neutral about language and platform, buying interoperability and portability.
  • Transparency is a family: access, location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure, persistence.
  • Scalability keeps the cost of physical resources, lost performance and bottlenecks under control, by decentralised algorithms, caching and replication.
ch1.js.1.3:
GFS, HDFS and BitTorrent are the three worked examples.

  • GFS: a single master holds the metadata, files are split into large chunks, and chunks are replicated across many chunk servers.
  • HDFS: a NameNode for metadata and many DataNodes holding replicated blocks, the descendant of GFS plus MapReduce.
  • BitTorrent: a file is split into pieces, and every peer that holds pieces also serves them.
  • Web search, commerce, healthcare, education and multiplayer games motivate the field.
ch1.js.1.4:
Three architecture models matter: client-server, peer-to-peer and multitier.

  • Architecture models describe the placement of the parts and the relationships between them.
  • Fundamental models describe the properties all architectures share.
ch1.js.the-three-characteristics-the-definition:
Three characteristics follow from the definition: concurrency, no global clock and independent failures.

  • Concurrency: programs on different machines share resources and run at the same time, so two nodes may want the same resource at the same moment.
  • No global clock: each machine has its own clock, so events are ordered by message passing, by Cristian's algorithm and NTP, or by Lamport's and vector clocks.
  • Independent failures: any component may fail without bringing the system down, so the system must tolerate partial failure.
ch1.js.further-characteristics:
Beyond those three, further properties are expected: Heterogeneity, Openness, Security, Scalability, Transparency and Fault tolerance.

  • Heterogeneity: components differ in network, hardware architecture, operating system, language and implementation, and still work together.
  • Openness: services are offered through published, standard interfaces, such as REST APIs.
  • Security: confidentiality, integrity and availability, harder here because parts travel over networks nobody controls.
  • Scalability grows in size, geography and administration; transparency hides the machines; fault tolerance masks failure.
ch1.js.advantages-and-disadvantages:
The advantages and the disadvantages are the same properties seen from opposite sides.

  • Advantages: economics, since microprocessors give better price and performance than one large machine; capacity added a machine at a time; data and resource sharing; flexibility.
  • Disadvantages: security is the main concern, since every node has to be secured; loss of data is possible while data moves; software is far more complex to develop; and distribution of control makes administration and fault-finding difficult.
ch1.js.main-problems-and-challenges:
Four goals exist because four problems do: heterogeneity, reliability, security and scalability.

  • Heterogeneity is masked by middleware, by internet protocols and by mobile code.
  • Reliability separates availability, the fraction of time the system is usable, from continuous operation; redundancy raises availability.
  • Security is confidentiality, integrity and availability, kept by encryption, authentication and authorisation.
  • Scalability is size, geographical and administrative; the symptoms are cost, lost performance, software resources and bottlenecks.
ch1.js.resource-sharing-and-what-a-service-is:
A resource is the thing itself; a service is the interface that manages a collection of related resources and decides who may use them and how.

  • Users share hardware such as a printer, data such as files, and specific functionality such as a search engine.
  • A file service offers read, write and delete on files rather than exposing the files themselves.
  • Services on other computers can only be invoked by communication.
ch1.js.the-web-as-a-distributed-system:
The Web's own difficulties are distribution problems seen in the wild.

  • Dangling links: a resource is deleted but links to it remain.
  • Slow response to web users.
  • Lack of a proper user interface.
ch1.js.client-server:
Client and server: the client sends a request asking for a service, and the server returns the result or an error code.

  • The request/reply runs over send/receive primitives, or through RPC or RMI.
  • Strength: one distinguished process owns the service, so one place controls access and knows the state.
  • Weakness: that server is a bottleneck and a single point of failure, and peers cannot be added to scale it.
ch1.js.peer-to-peer:
In the peer-to-peer model every process plays the same role, with no distinction between clients and servers.

  • A large number of data objects are shared, and any one computer holds only a small part of the application database.
  • Three problems follow: placing objects cleverly, retrieving the needed ones among many peers, and keeping the replicas equal.
  • Availability needs no distinguished server: no single node's failure ends the service.
  • BitTorrent shares files across the internet with no central server at all.
ch1.js.multitier:
Multitier extends the client-server idea into layers, so each tier can be scaled and replaced on its own.

  • The three-tier application: a presentation tier, an application or logic tier, and a data tier behind it.
  • Presentation holds what the user sees, application the decisions, data the state.
  • Split by function, one system serves thousands of clients from a handful of logic servers.
  • The data tier cannot simply be copied without asking how the copies are kept equal.
ch1.js.fundamental-models:
Three fundamental models describe the properties common to all the architecture models.

  • Interaction model: how processes communicate and coordinate, including the ordering of activities between them.
  • Failure model: classifies faults as omission, timing and arbitrary failures, so behaviour stays predictable when things break.
  • Security model: classifies forms of attack, as a basis for analysing threats.
  • A synchronous system bounds execution, message delivery and clock drift; an asynchronous one bounds nothing at all.
ch1.js.types-cluster-grid-and-cloud:
Distributed systems fall into three types: cluster, grid and cloud.

  • Cluster: interconnected stand-alone computers working cooperatively as one integrated resource; its key feature is homogeneity.
  • Grid: geographically distributed autonomous resources, shared and selected at runtime by availability, capability, performance, cost and quality of service; its five layers are fabric, connectivity, resource, collective and application.
  • Cloud: on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable resources, in the models SaaS, PaaS and IaaS.

ch3.js.3.0:
Time is the most important practical issue in distributed systems, and the most problematic.

  • Each computer has its own clock, so there is no single clock to read.
  • Clocks deviate, and they cannot be synchronized perfectly.
  • Without global physical time it is hard to say what state one process is in when another is in a given state.
  • Commerce still needs transactions timestamped consistently, and an execution read as an order of events.
ch3.js.3.1:
Clock synchronization splits into two families: physical clock synchronization and logical clock synchronization.

  • Physical: Cristian's algorithm for a centralized system and the Network Time Protocol for a distributed one.
  • Logical: Lamport timestamps and vector clocks, both distributed.
  • The clocks themselves are moved toward real time only in the first family; a logical clock is a counter that captures causal order numerically.
ch3.js.3.2:
Clock synchronization minimizes the difference between the accepted actual time and the time on a client machine.

  • Even so, relying on local clock time stays risky: a recorded time may have happened at a different time on another computer, because of differing drift rates.
  • Correcting time means the machines are much closer to each other on average, not that they all agree on time.
ch3.js.3.4:
Leader election designates one process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes.

  • Before it runs no node knows who will lead; afterwards every node recognizes the same unique leader.
  • It selects a master to take responsibility for averaging the time in the Berkeley algorithm.
  • It is needed at initialization of a central coordinator, or whenever the coordinator crashes, and in the token ring when the token holder fails.
  • A distributed algorithm assumes no coordinator exists: a master distributes sub-problems and collects the partial results.
ch3.js.how-a-computer-timer-actually-works:
A computer timer is a counter register and a holding register, decremented by a quartz crystal oscillator and reloaded at zero.

  • Each interrupt is a clock tick; the resulting physical clock counts oscillations at a definite frequency.
  • Drift rate is how fast a clock deviates from real time, and it decides how often to synchronize.
  • A synchronized clock must not deviate from real time by more than a certain amount.
  • Time is needed for performance measurement, recent data, temporal ordering, sender and receiver synchronization and shared access.
ch3.js.what-unsynchronized-clocks-break-the-mak:
The classic failure is make, which uses the clock of the machine it runs on to decide which source files need recompiling.

  • With the sources on a separate file server and unsynchronized clocks, it may treat an output as newer than its source and skip a rebuild that was needed.
  • The general statement: an event that occurred after another may be assigned an earlier time.
  • That is a correctness problem, not a performance problem.
ch3.js.event-ordering-and-the-happened-before-r:
With no common memory and no common clock, two events sometimes cannot be ordered by measurement, so order is defined without time.

  • The happened-before relation is a partial ordering from three rules: order within a process, send before receive, and transitivity.
  • Events not related by it are concurrent: no causal relationship between them.
  • A global order comes from timestamps where A → B implies ts(A) < ts(B).
  • The requirement is one-directional: a timestamp order does not prove a causal order.
ch3.js.causal-ordering-of-messages:
If M1 is sent before M2, every recipient of both must get M1 before M2, and the network does not promise that.

  • In a replicated database, updates must be received in order or the replicas diverge.
  • The fix is to buffer a later message until the earlier one it depends on has been delivered.
  • A message can take a different route and overtake an earlier one.
  • Lamport timestamps cannot decide dependency; vector clocks can.
ch3.js.cristian-s-algorithm:
Cristian's algorithm relies on a time server whose clock comes from a radio clock or other accurate source of UTC.

  • The client requests the time; the server replies with the time T from its own clock appended.
  • The client sets its clock to T + RTT/2, where RTT is the round-trip time of the request.
  • Both timestamps come from the client's clock, and the one-way delay is assumed to be half the round trip.
  • Accuracy is ± RTT/2, and the interrupt-handling time is a third quantity to subtract.
ch3.js.how-accurate-is-cristian-s-algorithm-exa:
The method assumes the round trip is split equally between request and response, a reasonable assumption on a LAN connection.

  • Accuracy improves by making multiple requests and using the response with the shortest RTT.
  • If min is the one-way transmission time, the server's time when the reply arrives lies between (T + min) and (T + RTT − min).
  • The width of that range is (RTT − 2·min), giving an accuracy of (RTT/2 − min).
  • The server must change its time gradually, by slewing the clock rather than setting it.
ch3.js.network-time-protocol-ntp:
NTP is the most commonly used internet time protocol and the one with the best accuracy.

  • Clients get updates from one or more servers and average them; the version that skips this is SNTP.
  • Servers listen on port 123 and reply with a UDP/IP packet carrying a 64-bit timestamp in UTC seconds since 1 Jan 1900.
  • Time sources form a synchronization subnet of strata: the first stratum connects directly to an accurate source, each below synchronized from the one above.
ch3.js.ntp-goals-and-synchronization-modes:
NTP's goals: accuracy to UTC despite message delays, filtering by statistics, reliable service, frequent synchronization, authentication.

  • Multicast is low accuracy, for quick LANs: the server periodically multicasts its time to its clients in the subnet.
  • Remote Procedure Call is medium accuracy: the server replies with its actual timestamp.
  • Symmetric mode is high accuracy, used to synchronize between the time servers, peer to peer.
  • All three are delivered unreliably over UDP, so the protocol needs many rounds and statistical filtering.
ch3.js.the-ntp-offset-derivation:
Four timestamps: T1 when the client sends, T2 when the server receives, T3 when the server responds, T4 when the client receives the response.

  • The client knows (T4 − T1) from its own clock, and the server reports T3 and T2.
  • Total transit time is (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2): elapsed time minus the time the server spent working.
  • With the transit time split equally, θ = [(T2 − T1) + (T3 − T4)] / 2.
  • Without that subtraction, server processing time is counted as network delay.
ch3.js.the-berkeley-algorithm-when-no-machine-h:
The Berkeley algorithm agrees on a time by averaging the machines' clocks: a time daemon asks every machine for the time, averages the answers, and tells each how to adjust.

  • Its server is active, where Cristian's and NTP's servers wait to be asked.
  • Nothing refers to real time, so it is internal synchronization, for a system with no UTC receiver.
  • The agreed time is only as good as the daemon's own clock, and the daemon itself is chosen by an election (3.4).
ch3.js.logical-clocks-the-idea:
A logical clock is a monotonically increasing software counter whose value need bear no particular relationship to any physical clock.

  • Each process keeps its own clock and uses it to apply Lamport timestamps to events, giving consistent event ordering.
  • The clocks only have to be internally consistent; a shared 10:00 is enough even if it is really 10:02.
  • Logical clocks live in the middleware layer, which timestamps on send and updates on receipt, so the application never touches a clock.
ch3.js.lamport-s-algorithm:
A Lamport logical clock is an incrementing software counter per process, with three rules.

  • A process increments its counter before each event in that process.
  • On sending the value travels with the message; on receiving, the counter is set above the maximum of its own value and the received one.
  • The result is a total order over all events, enough to order concurrent requests for one resource.
  • A smaller timestamp does not imply the event happened first: concurrent events can carry 3 and 7.
ch3.js.lamport-s-considerations-and-the-limitat:
Within a process no two events may share a timestamp, and a unique process ID may be needed to tell simultaneous events apart.

  • A system has partial order when a partial-order relationship exists among its events, and total order when causality relates them all.
  • In replicated systems, an update is timestamped at its accepting site and ordered by source timestamp at the receiver.
  • Lamport clocks give a total order consistent with causality, but ts(a) < ts(b) does not imply a → b.
ch3.js.vector-clocks:
A vector clock is an array of N logical clocks, one per process, which detects causality violations.

  • TS[i] at site i is the most recent value of site j's clock that site i has heard about.
  • An internal event increments the process's own clock in the vector; a send increments it and sends the whole vector.
  • A receive increments it again and takes the pairwise maximum with the received vector.
  • Two events are causally related exactly when one vector dominates the other, and non-dominating vectors are provably concurrent.
ch3.js.causal-ordering-of-messages-using-vector:
Causal ordering keeps the causal order of receives the same as the order of sends.

  • Two named algorithms: BSS causal ordering of broadcasts and SES causal ordering of regular messages.
  • Both delay an out-of-order message until the messages it depends on have been delivered.
  • To delay a message you must decide whether it is later than one still awaited, and Lamport timestamps cannot answer that; a vector timestamp can.
  • M1 causally precedes M2 exactly when M1's vector is dominated by M2's.
ch3.js.background:
Mutual exclusion is needed only where processes must exchange information to reach agreement.

  • One-way communication usually does not need it, and in client/server communication the server handles coordination, so the clients never interact.
  • A critical section is a region where a process competes destructively with another for a shared item.
  • A race condition comes from two processes entering that region at the same time.
  • Mutual exclusion is the solution: only one process enters the critical section at a time.
ch3.js.the-four-requirements:
The four requirements: safety, liveness, no starvation and fairness.

  • Safety: at most one process in the critical section.
  • Liveness: if more than one process is requesting, someone enters.
  • No starvation: a requesting process enters within a finite time.
  • Fairness: requests are granted in order, which implies no starvation and liveness; safety says what must never happen, the other three are claims about progress.
ch3.js.the-two-approaches-and-the-algorithm-fam:
Two families answer who may enter: permission-based and token-based.

  • Permission-based: every process competes freely, and requests are arbitrated by a central coordinator or by distributed agreement.
  • Named algorithms: a central coordinator, Lamport's, Ricart–Agrawala and the Token Ring.
  • Asking first costs messages and usually a wait on failure; holding a token costs nothing but must be found when lost.
ch3.js.ricart-agrawala-the-syllabus-s-named-non:
Ricart–Agrawala improves on Lamport's algorithm: a node need not send a REPLY when it holds a request with a lower timestamp.

  • No FIFO channels are required, because ordering is carried in the timestamps.
  • Cost: 2(n − 1) messages per critical-section invocation, a request to every other node and a reply from every other node.
  • Requests are granted in order of increasing timestamps; the synchronization delay is the maximum transmission time.
  • A node enters on replies from all nodes, then replies to the requests it deferred.
ch3.js.token-based-algorithms-and-the-token-rin:
A single token circulates, and whoever holds it may enter the critical section.

  • In the Token Ring algorithm the n processes form a logical ring, each holding the address of one neighbour clockwise.
  • A process waits for the token from its left neighbour, then passes it on clockwise.
  • Obtaining the token can take from 1 to n − 1 messages, and the worst case is a full lap.
  • It works well when heavily loaded; if the holder fails, a unique process must be elected to regenerate the token.
ch3.js.the-three-named-algorithms-side-by-side:
The three named algorithms trade cost against failure: the central coordinator is cheapest and most fragile, Ricart–Agrawala spreads the cost across every node, and the token ring makes the right to enter an object that can be lost.

  • Messages per entry and exit: 3, 2(n − 1), and 1 to n − 1 to obtain the token.
  • Delay before entry: 2 message times, the maximum message transmission time, and 0 to n − 1 hops.
  • What stops it: the coordinator's crash, an unreachable node, a lost token.
ch3.js.basic-concepts:
A unique priority number is associated with each active process, and the coordinator is always the process with the largest priority number.

  • When the coordinator fails, the active process with the largest priority number is elected; a crashed node cannot win.
  • The requirement is that one and only one process is chosen and that all agree on the decision.
  • Election starts after a failure, normally detected by a time-out.
  • Two phases: select the leader with the highest priority, then inform all processes of the winner.
ch3.js.the-bully-algorithm:
Bully elects the active process with the largest process ID where every process can reach every other.

  • Three messages: an election message, an answer that it is alive, and a coordinator message naming the winner.
  • A process finding the coordinator down messages every higher ID, and elects itself if none answers within T.
  • If a higher process answers, it waits T′ for that process to announce itself, then restarts if nothing arrives.
  • A recovered high-numbered process runs the algorithm at once and bullies a lower-numbered coordinator out.
ch3.js.the-ring-algorithm-chang-and-roberts:
Chang and Roberts elects the largest identification in a logical or physical ring.

  • It works for any number of processes N, with no process knowing the ring size.
  • A process that notices a lack of leader sends an election message with its own UID to its neighbour clockwise.
  • On receiving one, a process forwards a larger UID and replaces a smaller one it has not already forwarded.
  • When a UID returns to its own process, that process is the leader and sends an elected message round the ring.
ch3.js.bully-versus-ring-the-comparison:
The two agree on who wins, the largest identifier, and differ in what they assume.

  • Bully assumes every process can message every other, a mesh for example; the ring assumes unidirectional links to the right neighbour.
  • Bully sends election messages to every higher number, answers from the living, then a victory broadcast.
  • The ring costs one election message that accumulates ids and one coordinator message, two laps normally; bully needs each process to know the higher numbers, while the ring works for any N.

ch4.js.what-a-dfs-is:
A Distributed File System is a classical file system spread across multiple machines, sharing dispersed files.

  • Resources on another machine are remote; on the local machine they are local.
  • It enables programs to store and access remote files exactly as they do local ones.
  • Clients should view it the same way as a centralized file system, with the distribution hidden at a lower level.
  • Performance is judged by two numbers: throughput and response time.
ch4.js.the-design-goals:
Eight concepts, requirements and design goals apply to a DFS.

  • Transparency: the distribution is invisible, and remote files are used as local ones.
  • Concurrency, replication, heterogeneity and fault tolerance.
  • Consistency: all readers see updates according to a defined rule, despite caching and replication.
  • Security applies to remote files as strictly as to local ones, and efficiency means throughput and response time close to a local file system's.
ch4.js.transparency:
Transparency in a DFS is the family of properties applied to files.

  • The strict form is access transparency: the same operations on a remote file as on a local one, with the same result.
  • The others are location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure and persistence.
  • NFS is described as having access transparency as its design goal, where most other systems have something else.
ch4.js.naming-three-schemes-and-the-mapping-und:
Naming maps logical objects to physical ones, and the three schemes differ in location transparency.

  • Host plus local name: unique, but neither location transparent nor location independent.
  • Remote directories mounted to local ones: location independent, but the directories must be explicitly mounted — SUN NFS is the example.
  • A single global name structure spans all files, giving the strongest illusion of one system.
  • A transparent mapping goes name → file_identifier → <system, disk, cylinder, sector>, so moving a file changes only the unique identifier.
ch4.js.the-file-service-architecture:
The file service is structured into three components: the flat file service, the directory service and the client module.

  • The flat file service acts on the contents of files, referring to them by UFID.
  • The directory service maps text names to UFIDs, and supports creating directories and adding files.
  • The client module runs on each computer and gives applications a single API for both services.
  • It holds the network locations of the servers and caches recently used file blocks.
ch4.js.consistency-in-a-dfs:
Consistency is the requirement that all clients see the effects of updates by a defined rule when a file is replicated or cached.

  • It is unavoidable: caching is mandatory for performance, replication for availability, and concurrent access is normal.
  • The ends are strict consistency, where every read sees the most recent write at once, and relaxed consistency, where staleness is bounded.
  • NFS chooses relaxed consistency: close-to-open, with a consistency window of 30 seconds.
ch4.js.replication:
Replication means multiple copies of a file, and a transparent DFS returns a set of locations for the replicas.

  • Availability and fault tolerance: if one server or disk fails, another copy answers — the purpose in HDFS.
  • Performance: a read can be served by the nearest or least-loaded replica.
  • The systems differ: NFS minimal, Coda with read-one/write-all, Plan 9 none, xFS striping for bandwidth.
  • Replication has three motivations — availability, read performance and bandwidth — and consistency is the price of the first.
ch4.js.sun-nfs-what-it-is:
SUN NFS was developed by Sun Microsystems in 1985, the first commercially successful network file system.

  • It was developed for diskless workstations, and designed for robustness and adequate performance rather than the best possible performance.
  • Sun published all the protocol specifications, which is why NFS became a standard rather than a product.
  • It is both an implementation and a specification; its goal is to share a file system transparently.
  • It uses the client-server model, though a node can be both at once and there is no dedicated server.
ch4.js.stateful-versus-stateless-services:
NFS's most consequential decision is that it is stateless: every client request provides the complete information the server needs.

  • A stateful server keeps track of client requests — which files are open, connection identifiers, caches.
  • A stateful server performs better, since the filename is not parsed on every request.
  • A stateless server has nothing to reclaim or lose, so it recovers easily and the client simply retries.
  • Its cost is that every request repeats the lookup, which is why client caching compensates.
ch4.js.nfs-s-design-and-its-three-parts:
NFS's design has three parts: the protocol, the server side and the client side.

  • The protocol uses the Sun RPC mechanism and the Sun eXternal Data Representation (XDR), defined as a set of remote procedures.
  • The server's file handle holds a filesystem id, an i-node number and a generation number.
  • The client side gives a transparent interface: remote mount maps remote names to addresses, with VFS and VNODE calls.
  • Since the server is stateless, identity and access rights are checked on every request, which carries its userID and groupID.
ch4.js.hdfs-design-and-why-it-is-shaped-that-wa:
HDFS stores very large files with streaming data access, on clusters of commodity hardware.

  • Very large files: hundreds of megabytes to terabytes, with clusters holding petabytes.
  • Streaming access: the pattern is write-once, read-many-times, a dataset generated once then analysed many times.
  • Commodity hardware: node failure is expected, and HDFS carries on without a noticeable interruption.
  • It is a poor fit for low-latency data access, lots of small files, and multiple writers.
ch4.js.blocks:
HDFS has a block, a much larger unit: 64 MB by default, often 128 MB.

  • Files are broken into block-sized chunks stored as independent units.
  • A file can therefore be larger than any single disk, and the storage subsystem deals with blocks rather than files, which eliminates metadata concerns.
  • Blocks fit replication: each is replicated to a small number of separate machines, typically three.
  • Largeness minimises the cost of seeks: about 10 ms of seek against 100 MB/s gives about 100 MB.
ch4.js.namenodes-and-datanodes-the-architecture:
An HDFS cluster has a namenode as master and datanodes as workers.

  • The namenode manages the filesystem namespace: the tree and the metadata for all files and directories.
  • It knows which datanodes hold every block, and the data itself never passes through it.
  • Metadata is persisted as two files: the namespace image and the edit log.
  • Datanodes store and retrieve blocks when told to, and report the blocks they hold periodically.
  • A Secondary NameNode takes snapshots, keeping the namespace image and edit log from growing without bound.
ch4.js.why-the-namenode-is-a-single-point-of-fa:
If the machine running the namenode fails, all files would be lost, because nothing else knows how to reconstruct them.

  • Back up the state: the namenode writes its persistent state to multiple filesystems, synchronously and atomically.
  • A secondary namenode merges the namespace image with the edit log periodically, but does not act as a namenode.
  • HDFS Federation adds namenodes, each managing a portion of the namespace; they do not communicate, though datanodes register with all of them.
ch4.js.hdfs-high-availability-failover-and-fenc:
The namenode is still a single point of failure: if it fails, no client can read, write or list files.

  • Recovery the old way is a cold start that can take 30 minutes or more on large clusters.
  • High availability runs a pair of namenodes active-standby, so the standby takes over without significant interruption; it needs shared storage for the edit log, reports to both namenodes and client failover.
  • A failover controller manages the transition, and an ungraceful failover is made safe by fencing.
ch4.js.gfs-and-how-hdfs-relates-to-it:
HDFS was inspired by GFS, the Google File System.

  • Hardware failures are common, files are large and few, writes append.
  • High sustained bandwidth is preferred to low latency.
  • A single master holds the metadata, and many chunkservers hold fixed-size chunks of 64 MB with three replicas.
  • The read path: the client asks the master for the chunk handle and replica locations, caches them, then asks the closest replica.
  • An operation log recovers the master's state; chunk locations come from the chunkservers.
ch4.js.where-the-three-replicas-go-and-what-hap:
The placement rules for replicas are policy rather than a derivation: spread the copies across racks, prefer under-utilised chunkservers, and limit recent creations on each of them.

  • A rack is one failure domain, so copies in different racks survive the loss of a whole rack.
  • When the available replicas fall below the setting, the master tells a chunkserver to copy from a valid replica, with the clones and their bandwidth limited.
  • Three copies on one machine are one replica and two things that fail with it.
ch4.js.heterogeneity-and-why-middleware-exists:
Distributed applications are typically heterogeneous: different hardware, software, unconventional devices, and diverse networks and protocols.

  • It happens because different solutions suit different parts, users choose their own vendors, and legacy systems must keep working.
  • Middleware is a set of services that enable applications and end users to interact across a heterogeneous distributed system.
  • It resides above the network and below the application software.
  • Its two jobs: make the network transparent to users and applications, and hide the hardware, operating system and software details.
ch4.js.corba:
CORBA is the OMG's specification for an Object Request Broker.

  • It is a standard rather than a product, language-neutral and vendor-neutral, defined by an IDL.
  • Clients invoke through proxies and servers through skeletons, both generated from the IDL.
  • The interface repository holds the available interfaces, which is what makes dynamic invocation possible.
  • GIOP defines the messages exchanged between ORBs, and IIOP is its particularisation over TCP/IP.
  • Services include naming and trading, security, time, event and notification, transaction, and persistent objects.
ch4.js.java-rmi-as-middleware:
Java RMI is language-specific middleware: CORBA's interface is defined in a neutral language, while RMI's is the language itself.

  • RMI extends the Java object model to support distributed objects, letting objects invoke methods on remote objects with local syntax.
  • Type checking applies equally to remote and local calls, and a binder maps textual names to remote object references.
  • Its cost is that it is a single-language system, which is not enough in a heterogeneous estate.
ch4.js.messaging-middleware-mqtt-and-amqp:
The third family is message-oriented middleware: MQTT, AMQP, CoAP and XMPP.

  • MQTT is publish-subscribe messaging for lightweight devices over unreliable networks or intermittent connectivity, popular for IoT and M2M.
  • The publisher never names a receiver: a broker forwards data to interested subscribers and the topic decouples them.
  • Its overhead: a 1-byte control header and a 1-to-4-byte packet length, then an optional variable header and payload.
  • AMQP is a binary application-layer protocol for M2M messaging, supporting publish-subscribe and request-response with queues and exchanges.

ch5.js.5.3:
The three service models are a stack: Software as a Service, Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service.

  • IaaS gives the infrastructure — compute resources, CPU, VMs and storage — and the customer may run arbitrary software; Amazon EC2 is the example.
  • PaaS gives a platform on which to deploy applications using tools the provider supports; the customer controls only the application.
  • SaaS gives applications supplied by the provider, such as Gmail and Salesforce.
ch5.js.what-cloud-computing-is-the-two-definiti:
The two definitions name different things: the mechanism and the business model.

  • The infrastructure definition: ubiquitous access to shared pools of configurable system resources that can be rapidly provisioned with minimal management effort.
  • The business definition: the delivery of computing services over the Internet, charged by usage like a public utility.
  • Companies offering them are cloud providers.
  • The utility analogy is the defining attribute, and it is what separates cloud computing from hosting.
ch5.js.the-basic-reasoning-and-the-two-early-mo:
The reasoning: information and data processing can be done more efficiently on large farms of computing and storage systems accessible via the Internet.

  • Grid computing, from the National Labs in the early 1990s, targets scientific computing: resources from multiple locations pooled for a common goal.
  • Utility computing, from IT companies in 2005–2006, targets enterprise computing and charges for specific usage rather than a flat rate.
  • Grid contributes the pooling of resources for one goal; utility contributes billing by usage instead of buying.
ch5.js.the-five-technologies-and-the-timeline:
Five technologies made cloud computing what it is: distributed systems and their peripherals, virtualization, Web 2.0, service orientation and utility computing.

  • Virtualization supplies the isolation and multiplexing, so a provider can sell slices of one machine.
  • Web 2.0 supplies the browser-based interface, so a user needs nothing installed.
  • Service orientation supplies the interface idea, and utility computing the pricing.
  • The idea came in the 1950s and the result arrived in 2007.
ch5.js.the-three-axes-of-cloud-computing:
Three axes keep the unit's models apart.

  • Delivery (service) models: what the provider supplies — SaaS, PaaS and IaaS.
  • Deployment models: who the cloud is for and where the control sits — public, private, community, hybrid.
  • Defining attributes: what makes it cloud rather than ordinary hosting — utility pricing, Internet access and elasticity.
  • A fourth list names the resources the cloud is built from.
ch5.js.the-defining-characteristics:
Cloud computing offers on-demand, scalable and elastic computing, with resources metered and charged by use.

  • A shared pool of resources, with resource management.
  • Internet technology for scalable and elastic services; elastic computing acquires resources on demand to support a variable workload.
  • Metering, and cost-effectiveness from resource multiplexing passed on to users.
  • Scalability is the ability to handle growth; elasticity is acquiring and releasing resources automatically, which is the cloud's distinguishing property.
ch5.js.two-more-characteristics:
Two further characteristics are data storage and management.

  • Data storage: data is held in the cloud, closer to where it is used, and appears to users in a location-independent manner.
  • The storage strategy can increase reliability and security, and lower communication cost — location transparency applied to data.
  • Management: maintenance and security are operated by the providers, who are more efficient through specialisation and centralisation.
  • The objection is that relinquishing control becomes a security question.
ch5.js.the-benefits:
The benefits fall into four families: sharing, cost, capability and user convenience.

  • Sharing: CPU cycles, storage and bandwidth are shared, and peak demands do not coincide, so multiplexing raises utilisation.
  • Aggregation: resources can be aggregated for data-intensive work, and shared data facilitates collaboration.
  • Cost: no capital investment for a private infrastructure, and payment as you go for computing.
  • Capability and convenience: elasticity accommodates very large peak-to-average ratios, and virtualization lets users work in familiar environments.
ch5.js.challenges:
The challenges sit beside the advantages, one line each.

  • Availability of service: what happens when the provider cannot deliver?
  • Data confidentiality and auditability, described as a serious problem.
  • Vendor lock-in: diversity of services, data organisation and user interfaces limits user mobility.
  • A data transfer bottleneck, since many applications are data-intensive.
  • Performance unpredictability, resource management, and security for sensitive applications such as healthcare.
ch5.js.cloud-activities-what-a-provider-actuall:
A cloud service involves four families of activity.

  • Service management and provisioning: virtualization, provisioning, operations and systems management, QoS management, billing, SLA management and backups.
  • Security management: identity and authentication, intrusion prevention and detection, cryptography, physical security, access control, audit and trails, firewalls.
  • Customer services: assistance and online help, subscriptions, business intelligence, reporting.
  • Integration services: data management and development.
ch5.js.what-a-deployment-model-is:
A cloud deployment model is a specific configuration of environment parameters such as the accessibility and proprietorship of the infrastructure and storage size.

  • Deployment models define the type of access to the cloud — how the cloud is located.
  • A cloud can have four types of access: public, private, hybrid and community.
  • What separates them is not the hardware but who controls the infrastructure and where it sits.
  • The same physical data centre can be public for one customer and private for another.
ch5.js.the-four-models:
Four deployment models, separated by who controls the infrastructure.

  • Public cloud: available to the general public or a large industry group, owned by the organisation selling the services.
  • Private cloud: operated solely for one organisation, with little technical difference from a public one; also called internal or corporate.
  • Community cloud: shared by several organisations with shared concerns, whose difference from the private model is the set of users.
  • Hybrid cloud: two or more clouds bound by standardised technology enabling data and application portability.
ch5.js.the-comparison-table:
Read down a column and the four models are four settings of one trade: control against convenience.

  • The public cloud is cheapest and easiest to set up, giving up security, control and reliability.
  • The private cloud is the opposite in every one of those rows and the most expensive model.
  • The hybrid buys the elastic part from a public cloud while keeping the sensitive part in-house.
  • The community cloud shares the cost, and is the one row that is not high — fixed capacity.
ch5.js.advantages-disadvantages-and-use-cases-f:
Each model's advantages carry their own disadvantages and suit a particular use case.

  • Public: hassle-free management, high scalability and reduced cost, at the price of reliability and data privacy; for fluctuating demand.
  • Private: bespoke, flexible, secure and reliable, at considerable expense; for mission-critical operations under one company's control.
  • Community: cost reduction, improved security and collaboration, at a higher cost and with fixed capacity; for joint projects between organisations.
  • Hybrid: sensitive workloads stay private while the rest bursts to the public cloud.
ch5.js.ethical-issues-and-de-perimeterisation:
Moving to the cloud relinquishes control to third-party services and stores data on multiple sites.

  • The implications are unauthorized access, data corruption, and infrastructure failure and service unavailability.
  • De-perimeterisation is the removal of a boundary between an organisation and the outside world.
  • Systems and data are then protected on multiple levels, using encryption, secure protocols, secure systems and data-level authentication, rather than the network boundary.
  • Once the perimeter is gone, identity and access management and data-level security are the only controls left.

ch6.js.the-definition-and-why-it-is-the-foundat:
Virtualization runs multiple operating systems on a single physical system, sharing the underlying hardware.

  • It is the process by which one computer hosts the appearance of many computers.
  • Physical resources become a pool from which virtual resources are allocated, improving IT throughput and costs.
  • A virtual machine is an isolated runtime environment comprising a guest OS and its applications.
  • The stack is a physical box, a virtualization platform (Xen, KVM, VMware) and the virtual systems above it.
ch6.js.the-six-kinds-of-virtualization:
Six types of virtualization.

  • Application: the application is stored and run from a server, not the local machine.
  • Network: several virtual networks, each with a separate control and data plane, coexist on one physical network.
  • Desktop: the desktop and its applications are separated from the physical client device.
  • Storage: physical storage is aggregated into a pool that appears as one device.
  • Server: one physical server becomes several isolated virtual servers, each with its own operating system.
  • Data: many sources presented as one view.
ch6.js.the-hypervisor:
A hypervisor, also called a virtual machine manager, lets multiple operating systems share one hardware host.

  • Each guest appears to have the host's processor, memory and other resources to itself.
  • The hypervisor controls the host processor and resources, allocating what is needed to each system in turn.
  • It makes sure the guest operating systems cannot disrupt each other.
  • It sits directly between the physical hardware and its OS, supports hardware-level virtualization, and provides hypercalls to guests.
ch6.js.type-i-versus-type-ii:
The two types differ by one layer: Type I runs directly on the host, Type II runs as an application in a host system.

  • Type I, also called native or bare-metal, has direct access to hardware and is used in servers and data centres; Xen and KVM are examples.
  • Type II, also called hosted, reaches hardware through the host operating system and is used on desktops; VMware Workstation is an example.
  • A guest's I/O passes through two operating systems in the Type II case.
ch6.js.the-roles-of-a-hypervisor:
Five responsibilities, one per virtualized resource.

  • Isolating and emulating resources is the general responsibility.
  • CPU: scheduling virtual machines.
  • Memory: managing memory.
  • I/O: emulating I/O devices, which an unmodified operating system looks for and will not boot without.
  • Networking, and managing virtual machines.
ch6.js.cpu-virtualization:
A VM is a duplicate of a computer system, and most of its instructions execute on the host processor in native mode.

  • The rest are privileged instructions, which trap when executed outside privileged mode.
  • Control-sensitive instructions change the configuration of resources; behaviour-sensitive ones differ by configuration.
  • An architecture is virtualizable when those instructions are trapped in the VMM, which mediates hardware access from different VMs.
  • RISC virtualizes naturally; x86 needed binary translation, paravirtualization or hardware-assisted extensions.
ch6.js.memory-virtualization:
Virtual memory virtualization shares the system's RAM, allocating it dynamically to the VMs.

  • Traditionally the mapping from virtual to machine memory is one stage, through page tables.
  • Virtualized, it takes two: the guest OS maps virtual addresses to its own physical memory, and the VMM maps those to real machine memory.
  • The second stage exists so a guest cannot name memory belonging to another guest or the hypervisor.
  • The price is an extra translation on every access, which nested page tables recover.
ch6.js.i-o-virtualization:
Three approaches, each trading compatibility against overhead.

  • Full device emulation replicates device enumeration, identification, interrupts and DMA in software in the VMM, so unmodified guests work, at a very high overhead.
  • Direct I/O gives a VM direct access to devices, achieving close-to-native performance, though a reclaimed device may be left in an arbitrary state.
  • Hardware-assisted virtualization puts the remapping and isolation in hardware, since software emulation costs too much.
  • The virtual device remaps guest and real I/O addresses and multiplexes the physical device.
ch6.js.the-xen-architecture:
Xen is an open-source hypervisor developed by Cambridge University.

  • It is a micro-kernel hypervisor that separates policy from mechanism, leaving policy to Domain 0.
  • It includes no device drivers natively, only a mechanism by which a guest OS reaches the physical devices.
  • The guest OS with control ability is Domain 0; the others are Domain U.
  • Domain 0 is loaded first at boot and allocates and maps hardware resources for the guest domains.
ch6.js.benefits-of-virtualization:
Five benefits, each a cloud property restated at the machine level.

  • Sharing of resources: the multiplexing that makes pay-per-usage economical.
  • Isolation: virtual machines are isolated from each other as if physically separated, which is what makes multi-tenancy possible.
  • Encapsulation: a VM encapsulates a complete computing environment, so a whole machine becomes one file.
  • Hardware independence: VMs run independently of the underlying hardware.
  • Portability: VMs can be migrated between different hosts, which is what live migration is.
ch6.js.hypervisor-vulnerabilities-and-nohype:
Because the hypervisor sits between every guest and the hardware, it is a single point of attack that can see every guest.

  • The threat is malicious software running on the same server, attacking the hypervisor and reaching other VMs; the term is VM escape.
  • NoHype is one research answer: remove the hypervisor, and there is nothing to attack.
  • It still retains the needs of a virtualized cloud infrastructure.
  • The trade-off: the isolation the hypervisor provides is also the isolation it must be trusted to provide.
ch6.js.what-a-virtual-machine-is:
A virtual machine is a software program that emulates the functionality of physical hardware or a computing system.

  • It runs on top of the hypervisor, which replicates the underlying hardware resources in software.
  • The physical hardware is the host machine, and the VM running on it is the guest machine.
  • The VM contains what it needs to run its applications: storage, memory and networking.
  • A guest usually runs a complete operating system of its own, which is why a VM image is measured in gigabytes.
ch6.js.what-a-container-is:
Containerization creates abstraction at an OS level, letting several isolated workloads share the same physical resources.

  • A container is a unit of software that is lightweight but still bundles the code, its dependencies and the configuration into a single image.
  • Containers can run on bare-metal servers, on hypervisors, or in cloud infrastructure.
  • The defining difference: a containerization engine creates isolated environments within the same host system kernel, separate only in their binaries and libraries.
  • That is what makes them more resource-efficient compared to VMs.
ch6.js.the-comparison-and-the-costs-on-each-sid:
Both virtualize, at different levels: a VM virtualizes the machine, a container the operating system.

  • A VM's abstraction is at hardware level; a container's is at operating-system level, so it sees a user space.
  • A VM instance includes a full guest operating system; a container image includes only the code, dependencies and configuration.
  • Containers are more resource-efficient and faster to start, but less secure, because the underlying operating system is shared.
  • VMs can run different guest operating systems; all containers on a host run atop the same kernel.
ch6.js.the-provider-s-four-layers:
The provider is drawn in layers: service, resource abstraction and control, and physical resource, with management beside them.

  • Service layer: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS — the three delivery models as the customer sees them.
  • Resource abstraction and control layer: the hypervisors, virtual machines and control software — where virtualization lives.
  • Physical resource layer: hardware and facility — servers, storage, network, power, cooling and physical security.
  • Cloud service management: business support, provisioning and configuration, portability and interoperability.
  • Security, privacy and performance run vertically through all three.
ch6.js.the-actors-the-nist-reference-model-s-te:
The NIST reference model names six actors.

  • Consumer: the principal stakeholder that maintains a business relationship with the provider.
  • Provider: the entity that makes services available.
  • Auditor: conducts an audit to express an opinion, verifying conformance to standards; SLA verification depends on it.
  • Broker: manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates between providers and consumers, through intermediation, aggregation and arbitrage.
  • Developer builds applications on the provider's platform, and Carrier provides the connectivity.
ch6.js.the-provisioning-problem-and-the-sla-ten:
Providers supply cloud services by signing SLAs with end users, committing enough CPU, memory and bandwidth for a preset period.

  • Underprovisioning leads to broken SLAs and penalties.
  • Overprovisioning leads to resource underutilisation and a decrease in revenue.
  • So provisioning is a commercial optimum rather than a technical one.
  • Five sources of difficulty: unpredictable consumer demand, software and hardware failures, heterogeneity of services, power management, and conflicts between the signed SLAs.
ch6.js.efficient-vm-provisioning:
Efficient VM provisioning depends on the cloud architecture and on managing cloud infrastructures.

  • In a virtualised cluster it demands three capabilities: efficient installation of VMs, live VM migration, and fast recovery from failures.
  • Users treat VMs as physical hosts with customised operating systems for specific applications.
  • Amazon EC2 uses Xen as the virtual machine monitor, the same VMM as IBM's Blue Cloud, and provides predefined VM templates.
  • IBM's Blue Cloud provides no templates; Microsoft applies virtualization in Azure.
ch6.js.the-three-provisioning-methods:
Three provisioning methods: demand-driven, event-driven and popularity-driven.

  • Demand-driven adds or removes instances by utilisation: below a threshold decrease capacity, above it increase.
  • Easy to implement, but it fails when the workload changes abruptly — by the time the threshold is crossed, the capacity is needed.
  • Event-driven anticipates a specific time event, such as Christmastime, and works well if the event is predicted correctly.
  • Popularity-driven creates instances for currently popular applications, with the same risk of wasted resources if traffic does not occur.
ch6.js.the-software-stack-and-runtime-support:
Two closing ideas about cloud architecture.

  • The software stack is built from scratch for rigorous goals, so every layer is designed for high throughput, high availability and fault tolerance.
  • The lower layers are not completely transparent to the upper layers, because each layer sells a different thing.
  • Runtime support services: cluster monitoring collects the runtime status of the whole cluster, and a scheduler queues tasks and assigns them to nodes by availability.
  • The distributed scheduler has special characteristics, such as scheduling programs written in MapReduce style.
ch6.js.cloud-service-tasks-and-trends:
A short list for a question on the current state of the cloud.

  • SaaS is the top layer for business applications; CRM offered the first successful SaaS on the cloud.
  • SaaS tools also serve distributed collaboration, financial and human-resources management.
  • PaaS is provided by Google, Salesforce.com and Facebook among others; IaaS by Amazon, Windows Azure and Rackspace.
  • Collocation services require multiple providers to work together to support supply chains in manufacturing.
  • Network cloud services provide communications, from AT&T, Qwest and AboveNet.

ch7.js.what-a-cloud-platform-is:
A cloud provider is a company offering computing services over the Internet and charging for them by usage.

  • The platform is the whole of what that provider offers: the three delivery models in one catalogue.
  • IaaS comes from Amazon, Windows Azure and Rackspace; PaaS from Google, Salesforce.com and Facebook.
  • EC2 is the IaaS example, Google App Engine and Windows Azure the PaaS examples, Gmail and Salesforce the SaaS examples.
  • Three questions of any platform: what is rented, where it is, and how it is billed.
ch7.js.the-three-platforms:
AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the three platforms.

  • AWS: the first mover and largest catalogue; EC2 uses Xen as its virtual machine monitor; S3 is object storage; Lambda is serverless.
  • Azure: began as a managed application platform, then expanded into virtual machines and SaaS.
  • Google Cloud: began with App Engine and expanded into virtual machines and Kubernetes.
  • Each now offers virtual machines, containers, functions and object storage, so the choice is geography, price and ecosystem.
ch7.js.what-an-iaas-provider-actually-supplies:
The services of a cloud platform, by layer.

  • Compute: virtual central processing units and virtual main memory for the VMs provisioned to end users.
  • Storage: the provider supplies back-end storage for storing files.
  • Network: Network as a Service provides routers, switches and bridges for the VMs.
  • Load balancers: load balancing capability at the infrastructure layer.
  • Top providers include Amazon Web Services, Rackspace, Netmagic Solutions, Tata Communications, Sify Technologies and Reliance.
ch7.js.the-advantages-and-disadvantages-of-the-:
The customer's view of a rented platform.

  • Advantages: shared infrastructure, web access to the resources, a pay-as-per-use model, focus on the core business, and on-demand scalability.
  • Disadvantages: security, since most providers cannot give 100% security.
  • Maintenance and upgrade: providers maintain the software but do not upgrade it for some organisations.
  • Interoperability: migrating a VM from one provider to another is difficult, so customers face vendor lock-in.
ch7.js.the-pizza-analogy-which-makes-the-three-:
The delivery models as four ways of getting pizza.

  • On-premises: dined in at home — the customer manages everything.
  • IaaS: take and bake — the vendor supplies the dough, sauce, toppings and cheese; the customer supplies the table, oven and fire.
  • PaaS: pizza delivered — the vendor brings the finished pizza; the customer provides the table and the drinks and manages only the application.
  • SaaS: dined out — everything is the restaurant's, and the customer manages only its data and its account.
ch7.js.the-wider-family-xaas:
XaaS — Anything as a Service — delivers anything over a network rather than locally.

  • HaaS: managed service providers own hardware and install it at customers' sites on demand.
  • CaaS: VoIP, instant messaging and video conferencing hosted in the vendor's cloud.
  • DaaS: desktops delivered as virtual services, with the provider backing up the data.
  • SECaaS: outsourced security management — anti-virus, encryption, authentication.
  • DBaaS: a database platform through the cloud; TaaS: transport applications paid for by distance.
ch7.js.the-three-shapes-of-cloud-storage:
S3 and Blob are both object storage, in three shapes.

  • Object storage: objects in a flat namespace, each addressed by a key, used through an HTTP API — PUT an object, GET an object.
  • Block storage: volumes of raw blocks attached to a virtual machine, which the guest OS formats with a file system.
  • File storage: files in directories, mounted as a shared directory by several instances.
  • AWS: S3, EBS and EFS; Azure: Blob Storage, Managed Disks and Azure Files; Google: Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk and Filestore.
ch7.js.how-object-storage-is-actually-shaped:
Both S3 and Blob behave alike.

  • A bucket or container is the top-level namespace: the unit of policy and naming.
  • An object is addressed by key within its bucket; there are no real directories.
  • Metadata: name, modification time and access control list, plus four kilobytes of user fields.
  • The API is HTTP verbs on a URL — PUT, GET, DELETE — so the interface is REST.
  • Durability comes from replication; availability is separate: 99.999999999%.
  • Tiers trade retrieval cost against storage cost; lifecycle rules move objects between tiers.
ch7.js.databases-as-a-service:
Database as a Service provides access to a database platform through the cloud; AWS and Azure both have offerings.

  • The distinction is who administers the database.
  • On a rented virtual machine it is IaaS with your own DBMS on top: you size it, patch it, back it up and run its replicas.
  • A managed database keeps the platform and removes the administration: provisioning, maintenance, replication, indexing and tuning.
  • Two families: relational (SQL, schemas, transactions, joins) and non-relational (key-value, document, wide-column, graph).
  • Course examples: SimpleDB and Bigtable, both non-relational.
ch7.js.the-three-shapes-of-compute:
Compute comes in three shapes, differing in how much of the stack the customer manages.

  • Virtual machines: EC2, Azure Virtual Machines and Compute Engine; the customer manages the guest OS, patches, runtime and scaling.
  • Containers: ECS, AKS and GKE; the customer manages the image and the orchestration, and the orchestrator schedules it.
  • Serverless functions: Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Functions; the customer manages only the code, started by an event and billed per invocation.
  • Each step removes a layer the customer patches, scales and pays for.
ch7.js.ec2-the-virtual-machine-service:
EC2 is a web service providing elastic computing power.

  • Xen is its VMM, the same one as IBM's Blue Cloud, with predefined VM templates (AMIs).
  • Instance: one running VM; instance type: its CPU, memory and network profile. Security group: its firewall rules.
  • Lifecycle: launch, run, stop and start, reboot, terminate. The public IP returns to the pool on stop or terminate; an elastic IP does not.
  • On-demand, reserved and spot: per second, a commitment for a discount, or reclaimable spare capacity.
  • Auto-scaling is demand-driven provisioning implemented as a service.
ch7.js.lambda-the-serverless-service:
Serverless means the provider runs the code; the customer does not manage servers.

  • A trigger starts a fresh execution environment, reused while traffic continues; no copy stays running when it stops, and billing is per invocation.
  • Scaling is per request and automatic: the platform runs as many copies as the traffic needs.
  • Functions are stateless between invocations, so state belongs in storage or a database.
  • The trade, pushed further: no OS to configure, execution time capped, and cold starts add latency.
ch7.js.gce-and-why-the-three-platforms-look-ali:
Google Compute Engine is the counterpart of EC2 and Azure Virtual Machines.

  • Instances from images, attached persistent disks, a virtual network with firewall rules and load balancing.
  • Its distinguishing feature is the ecosystem around it: the Kubernetes origins and the data and machine-learning services on top.
  • All three converge because the services are APIs, and a widely used API becomes a de facto standard.
  • So lock-in is partial: the concepts transfer, but the management APIs, identity model and proprietary services do not.
ch7.js.managing-a-platform:
A platform is used through a console, an API, a CLI and SDKs.

  • It is organised by region, a geographic area, and availability zone, an isolated set of data centres within it.
  • That is a fault-domain rule: place replicas across zones so one zone's failure is survivable.
  • The provider's own requirements are the reference architecture: orchestration, resource abstraction and control, physical resources and management.
  • Its software stack is designed for high throughput, high availability and fault tolerance, each layer providing an interface above.

ch8.js.the-three-states-of-data-and-how-each-is:
Security covers four things, three of them the states data can be in.

  • Data-in-transit — confidentiality and integrity from a secured protocol (TLS) or from encrypting the payload.
  • Data-at-rest — generally not encrypted, being commingled with other users' data; encryption defeats indexing.
  • Data-in-use — processing, including multitenancy: the data must be readable, so platform trust is not replaced by cryptography.
  • Data lineage — when and where the data was: identifier, timestamp, endpoint.

Homomorphic encryption and predicate encryption aim at confidentiality and searchability together.
ch8.js.data-provenance-the-question-security-ca:
Data provenance extends lineage into computational accuracy as well as data integrity.

  • The exchange rate, the system's location and the state of the machine are all unverifiable to the customer.
  • The workload ran on a machine the customer does not own, in a jurisdiction they may not know, at a time they cannot check.
  • Integrity of data is not integrity of computation: the bytes can be untouched while the result is wrong.
ch8.js.data-remanence-and-the-provider-s-own-da:
