Data remanence is the risk of inadvertent disclosure — data that remains where it was not intended to remain.

  • It connects to storage virtualization: if you do not know which physical disks hold your blocks, proving a deleted copy is gone is harder.
  • Centralisation: quantities of data from many companies make the collection an attractive target for criminals.
  • Physical security of the data centre and the trustworthiness of system administrators become the customer's risk.
ch8.js.data-privacy:
Privacy varies among countries, cultures and jurisdictions, shaped by public expectations and legal interpretations, so a concise definition is elusive.

  • Privacy rights concern the collection, use, disclosure, storage and destruction of personal data (PII), and come down to accountability of organisations and transparency of their practices.
  • The five concerns: storage, retention, destruction, auditing and breaches — with data residency among the storage questions.
ch8.js.compliance-and-the-data-life-cycle:
Compliance is managed over a data life cycle, and two rules govern it: personal information is managed as part of the organisation's data, and protection must consider the cloud's impact at each phase.

  • The seven phases: generation, transformation, transfer, use, storage, archival, destruction.
  • The cloud changes the risk at each: transfer crosses legal regimes, use needs the data readable, and destruction is a request to a provider rather than an act.
ch8.js.what-iam-is:
IAM is a framework of policies and technologies that ensures the right individuals get the right access to the right resources.

  • Authentication verifies identity (username/password, multi-factor authentication).
  • Authorization defines permissions and actions.
  • User management handles accounts, groups and roles — permissions attach to roles at cloud scale.
  • Policy enforcement applies the security policies; audit logs and monitors activity.

One identity spanning services is federated identity and single sign-on in practice.
ch8.js.why-iam-matters-more-in-the-cloud-than-o:
A familiar topic becomes a different problem in the cloud, for five reasons.

  • The organisation's trust boundary becomes dynamic and moves beyond its control, into the provider's domain.
  • Access must serve diverse user populations — employees, contractors, partners — with more authentication demanded.
  • Higher-assurance authentication is needed, as authentication may happen outside the firewall and passwords have limits.
  • Users authenticate from mobile devices, over networks the organisation does not control.

The control becomes identity rather than network location.
ch8.js.authentication-and-authorisation-named:
The order between the two halves of IAM matters.

  • AuthN — authentication, answering who is asking.
  • AuthZ — authorisation, answering what that identity may do; authentication without it leaves a verified identity with everything.
  • Role-based access control — a user logs in with a role, and the role determines the protection domain; one person may hold several roles at once.
  • Least privilege — an identity holds the permissions its function requires and no others, enforced by deny-by-default and short-lived credentials.
ch8.js.what-an-sla-is:
An SLA is the service contract with the provider: a guaranteed minimum level and a target level, with metrics and service objectives.

  • A complete statement names the service, the metric, the minimum and the target, plus the remedy when the minimum is missed.
  • An SLA is per service: compute, storage, networking and support agreements cover one account at once.
  • The remedy is usually a service credit, not compensation for lost business.

Meeting the minimum means no breach, not good service.
ch8.js.the-five-sla-criteria:
The five criteria, and what each measures:

  • Availability — percentage of time the service is guaranteed to be available.
  • Performance — response time and throughput.
  • Disaster recovery — mean time to recover.
  • Problem resolution — the process for identifying problems, support options and resolution expectations.
  • Security and privacy of data — mechanisms for data in storage and transmission.

Availability is a percentage of a period: 99.9% of a thirty-day month is about 43 minutes, and 99.99% is about 4.3 minutes.
ch8.js.the-five-phases-of-the-sla-life-cycle:
The five phases of the contract's life, from identification of terms to termination:

  • Contract definition — offerings and SLAs defined from standard templates, forming a catalogue.
  • Publishing and discovery — the offerings are advertised and customers search the catalogue.
  • Negotiation — terms agreed and signed off.
  • Operationalization — SLA monitoring, accounting and enforcement, with policies expressible in CIM.
  • De-commissioning — termination of all activities under the SLA.
ch8.js.the-five-phases-of-sla-management-in-the:
This is the life of the hosted application rather than of the contract:

  • Feasibility — a study of technical, infrastructure and financial feasibility.
  • On-boarding — the application moves to the platform and is profiled to create policies for its SLOs.
  • Pre-production — a simulated production environment where the customer validates the findings.
  • Production — the application is live; sustained breaches return it to on-boarding.
  • Termination — data returns to the customer, with only essential information kept.
ch8.js.the-eight-common-vulnerabilities:
The eight vulnerabilities:

  • Data breaches — unauthorized access through misconfigured storage, weak access controls or poor encryption.
  • Insecure APIs — weak authentication or input validation; the API surface is the attack surface.
  • Misconfigurations — overly permissive buckets, open security groups, weak firewall rules.
  • Account hijacking — compromised credentials abused to exfiltrate data or abuse resources.
  • DoS / DDoS — elastic capacity means an attack can be billed to the victim.
  • Insider threats, shared technology risks and legal risks complete the eight.
ch8.js.the-eight-mitigation-control-areas:
The eight control areas, with their practices:

  • Data security — encrypt in transit and at rest; manage keys with KMS/HSM.
  • Identity & access management — least privilege, MFA, short-lived credentials, deny-by-default.
  • Secure APIs — OAuth 2.0 / JWT, input validation, rate limiting, a WAF.
  • Configuration management — posture management, vulnerability scans, policy as code.
  • Threat detection & monitoring — centralised logging and SIEM, anomaly detection.
  • DoS/DDoS resilience, vendor diligence and training make up the eight.
ch8.js.the-shared-responsibility-model-and-the-:
The shared responsibility model is the division of duty.

  • The provider secures the cloud — the physical facility, the hardware, the hypervisor and the managed services underneath.
  • The customer secures in the cloud — their configuration, identities, data and code.
  • That is why misconfiguration and insecure APIs are the customer's fault even though the platform is the provider's.

The provider can certify the platform; knowing which side of the line each control sits on is the customer's job.
ch8.js.how-the-four-sub-topics-fit-together:
A long security question structures as a chain of five links:

  • The risks — the eight vulnerabilities and the exposures of the four data states.
  • The obligations — privacy and PII, retention, destruction, compliance and residency.
  • The controls — the eight control areas, with IAM and encryption as the data controls.
  • The assurance — the SLA, its breach and penalty machinery, and the auditor who verifies it.
  • The division of duty — shared responsibility and de-perimeterisation.

Shared responsibility and shared technology carry the most weight.
ch8.js.the-two-challenges-worked-through:
Two challenges, each with its mechanism and its mitigation.

  • Multi-tenancy and shared technology — tenants share hardware and a hypervisor, so a hypervisor flaw can enable cross-tenant attacks, and centralised data makes the collection an attractive target. Mitigation: patching and isolation, least privilege, monitoring, provider certification.
  • Data confidentiality and the limits of control — data-at-rest is generally not encrypted, governments may search data by residency, and replication makes proof of destruction hard. Mitigation: encryption with managed keys, tokenisation, residency-aware regions, contractual retention and deletion terms, and audit.

ch9.js.why-computation-moved-out-of-the-data-ce:
Cloud computing consolidated resources; the counter-movement is driven by physics.

  • Sending all device data to a distant data centre costs latency, bandwidth and sometimes privacy or legal compliance, and fails entirely when the device is offline.
  • The progression: content at the edge (the content-delivery network), then edge servers assisting, then fog computing, where end-user devices form part of the system.
ch9.js.the-three-tiers:
Compute is placed where latency and bandwidth allow it, and only what must be central is central.

  • Edge — the devices themselves: milliseconds, tiny compute, real-time control and offline operation.
  • Fog — nodes near the edge: gateways, cell towers, on-premise servers, one local network hop, shared by many devices.
  • Cloud — the data centre: the elastic pool, unlimited capacity and global reach, for training, archives and heavy analytics.

The tiers differ by where the compute sits relative to the data source, not by what technology they use.
ch9.js.what-the-trends-actually-buy:
What the move to the edge buys, and what it costs.

  • Latency — a control loop cannot wait for a round trip to another continent.
  • Bandwidth and cost — filtering at the edge is the difference between sending events and sending video.
  • Privacy and compliance — processing where the data was produced keeps regulated data inside a jurisdiction.
  • Availability — a device that keeps working without connectivity keeps working.
  • The costs: many more nodes to manage, weaker physical security, updates across a fleet, and clock synchronisation between thousands of devices.
ch9.js.what-serverless-means:
Serverless computing is a model in which the provider runs the code and the customer provisions no servers.

  • FaaS — event-driven execution billed per invocation; the platforms are AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google Cloud Functions.
  • BaaS — managed databases, queues, authentication and storage that a function calls instead of running its own.
  • The properties: event-driven, no server management, automatic scaling, pay per use, and stateless functions.
  • The trade: control is given up for convenience, and steady high load is cheaper on a reserved machine.
ch9.js.where-serverless-is-the-right-answer:
Where serverless fits, and where it does not.

  • Glue between services — a file arriving in storage triggers a resize or an index update.
  • Scheduled and administrative jobs — nightly reports, cleanup, backups: minutes of work a day.
  • Sporadic traffic — an internal tool, a webhook endpoint, or an API used in bursts.
  • An event-driven application — each step of a workflow consumes the previous step's event.
  • Wrong for long-running processes, stateful services, latency-critical workloads where a cold start is unacceptable, and steady high load.
ch9.js.docker-and-the-container-it-runs:
A container is a unit of software that is lightweight but still bundles the code, its dependencies and the configuration into a single image.

  • Unlike a virtual machine it shares the host system kernel, and is therefore more resource-efficient.
  • Image — the packaged unit, frozen; Dockerfile — the recipe that builds it, so the environment is reproducible.
  • Registry — where images are stored and fetched, so a build becomes a deployment.
  • Container engine — what runs the container — on bare metal, on hypervisors or in cloud infrastructure.
ch9.js.why-an-orchestrator-is-needed:
A production system is many containers across many machines, and Docker does not solve four problems.

  • Placement — which container runs on which node; restarts and self-healing — replacing what crashes.
  • Scaling — adding copies when load rises; networking and discovery — callers need a stable name.
  • Kubernetes solves them by declaring the desired state and continuously working to match it.
  • A pod is the smallest deployable unit, a service a stable name in front of a changing set of pods, and managed Kubernetes the provider running the control plane.
ch9.js.the-security-caveat:
Containers are not free isolation: the cons include less security from sharing the operating system.

  • A virtual machine's boundary is enforced by the hypervisor; a container's by the kernel it shares with its neighbours, so any kernel flaw crosses it — Meltdown was one.
  • The first process normally runs as root, so an escape yields root on the host.
  • Hardening: run as a non-root user, drop unneeded capabilities, mount read-only, apply a seccomp or AppArmor profile, and patch the host kernel.
ch9.js.what-cloud-native-means:
Cloud-native treats the cloud's properties as given rather than as a place to host something built for a server.

  • The application assumes the platform is elastic, programmable, failure-prone and disposable, so it is built from small independently deployable services.
  • Lift-and-shift inherits the cloud's costs without its benefits; cloud-native changes the design so elasticity, self-healing and pay-per-use are usable.
  • The characteristics: microservices, containers, orchestration, declarative configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous delivery, observability and horizontal scaling.
ch9.js.microservices-and-the-monolith-they-repl:
A microservice architecture structures an application as small independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over a network interface.

  • Versus a monolith: scaling is per service rather than the whole application; deployment is independent; each service can use its own technology; a fault is contained.
  • The cost: each service owns its data, so consistency across services replaces distributed transactions, and partial failure becomes normal.
  • The real cost is distributed systems — splitting an application converts local calls into remote calls, bringing latency, marshalling and call semantics.
ch9.js.how-containers-and-orchestration-support:
The support is an argument in four steps rather than a stack.

  • Microservices create the need for packaging: each service must arrive with its dependencies intact.
  • Packaging creates the need for orchestration: an image is static, so something must place it and keep the copies alive.
  • Many moving services create the need for delivery and observability, because failures are partial and not visible on one machine.
  • Each step costs: remote calls, a weaker boundary than a hypervisor's, and an orchestration layer that is itself a distributed system.
ch9.js.the-trend-list-in-the-syllabus-s-own-ter:
Four trends, one line each.

  • Edge and fog computing — moving computation toward the data source, to cut latency and bandwidth.
  • Serverless architecture — functions and managed backends the customer does not provision, billed per invocation.
  • Kubernetes and Docker — Docker packages an application into an image; Kubernetes schedules, heals and scales those containers.
  • Cloud-native and microservices — designing for the cloud's properties: small services, containers, orchestration.
  • The distinction: edge and fog move computation; the other three change how an application is built.
ch9.js.how-the-trends-connect-to-each-other:
The trends are one arc: consolidation into the cloud, the problems it creates, then distribution back out.

  • Edge and fog ask the deployment question harder: what if the cloud came to the data?
  • Serverless completes the compute ladder — EC2 the OS, containers the runtime, functions the process lifetime.
  • Containers and Kubernetes continue the virtualisation discussion past the hypervisor, at cluster scale.
  • Cloud-native and microservices use the fundamental challenges: heterogeneity, concurrency and partial failure become normal.
  • Every trend moves a problem rather than deleting it.
ch9.js.cloud-native-architecture-the-definition:
The topic has two halves: what cloud-native architecture is, and how each tool supports it.

  • What it is — the definition, the characteristics (microservices, containers, orchestration, declarative configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous delivery, observability, horizontal scaling), and the contrast with lift-and-shift.
  • How each tool supports it — microservices provide the structure, containers the packaging, and orchestration the operation that keeps the declared replica count alive and replaces what fails.
